intro: Eight cases that get harder as you go, from a spot on the tongue to advanced cancers and survivorship care. Each starts with a one-liner, then gives you more information step by step: exams, scopes, and scans, the stage, the treatment, the nodal levels, the landmark trials, and the side effects to counsel on. Some steps are multiple choice, some are fill-in-the-blank. Staging uses the AJCC 8th edition, as in the NCCN Head and Neck Guidelines.

cases.title: Case 1: The Spot on the Tongue
cases.oneLiner: A 57-year-old man who smokes a pack a day and drinks four beers a night is sent by his dentist for a painless white patch on the left side of his tongue. It has been there for about 3 months.

steps.label: Exam
steps.caption: The lesion on exam: a white plaque on the left lateral tongue. Coronation Dental Specialty Group, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
steps.prompt: The patch is about 1 cm, does not scrape off with a tongue blade, and is not tender. There are no neck nodes. What is the best next step?
choices: Reassure him: white patches in the mouth are usually benign
Two weeks of antifungal treatment, then recheck in 6 months
Refer for radiation to the oral tongue
steps.explanation: A white patch that does not wipe off (leukoplakia) or a red patch (erythroplakia) gets a biopsy, not reassurance. Thrush wipes off; this does not. The lateral tongue is the most common site of oral cavity cancer, and his tobacco and alcohol use raise the stakes.

steps.label: Risk factors
steps.prompt: Which of these is mainly a risk factor for a different head and neck subsite, not the oral cavity?
steps.explanation: High-risk HPV drives oropharynx cancer (tonsil and base of tongue). Oral cavity cancer is the classic tobacco, alcohol, and betel nut cancer. Even a p16-positive oral tongue cancer is still staged as oral cavity, not oropharynx.

steps.label: Biopsy
steps.context: Incisional biopsy: keratosis with severe epithelial dysplasia. No invasive carcinoma.
steps.prompt: Is this a cancer, and does he need radiation?
steps.answer: No. This is a premalignant lesion (leukoplakia with dysplasia), not invasive cancer, so there is nothing to stage and no role for radiation.
steps.explanation: Management is removal of the lesion when feasible, stopping tobacco and alcohol, and close surveillance with a re-biopsy of anything that changes. A radiation oncologist only meets this patient if an invasive cancer develops.

steps.label: Counseling
steps.prompt: He asks how likely a white patch like this is to turn into cancer. Using the figure from the epidemiology reading, what is the risk over about 10 years?
steps.explanation: Leukoplakia carries roughly a 1-20% risk of malignant transformation over 10 years, and dysplasia (especially severe dysplasia) sits at the higher end. That is why he stays in surveillance and why quitting smoking matters.

steps.label: If it progresses
steps.prompt: Two years later an ulcer appears at the same spot and biopsy shows invasive squamous cell carcinoma. What is the standard first treatment for an oral tongue cancer, and why not radiation alone?
steps.answer: Surgery first: a partial glossectomy with negative margins plus a neck dissection, with radiation added afterward only for adverse pathologic features.
steps.explanation: Oral cavity cancer is surgery-first territory. Radiation alone does poorly here and puts the mandible at risk of osteoradionecrosis.

cases.title: Case 2: The Raspy Voice
cases.oneLiner: A 66-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history has had a hoarse voice for 4 months. He has no trouble swallowing or breathing and has not noticed any neck lumps.

steps.label: Localize
steps.prompt: Which part of the larynx best explains persistent hoarseness as the first and only symptom?
steps.explanation: Even a small tumor on a true cord changes the voice, so glottic cancer tends to be caught early. Supraglottic cancer presents later with sore throat, trouble swallowing, or a neck mass; subglottic cancer with stridor or airway symptoms.

steps.label: Scope
steps.context: Flexible laryngoscopy: an irregular, exophytic lesion on the left true vocal cord that extends up onto the left false cord (supraglottis). The left cord still moves, but less than the right. Biopsy: invasive squamous cell carcinoma. CT neck: no cartilage invasion, no paraglottic space involvement, no enlarged nodes.
steps.caption: Laryngoscopy showing a lesion on the left vocal cord. Crosetti E et al., Curr Oncol Rep 2024 (PMC11168980), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: Stage this cancer (AJCC 8th edition, glottic larynx).
steps.explanation: Glottic T2 means spread to the supraglottis and/or subglottis, and/or impaired cord mobility. He has both. A fixed cord (or paraglottic space or inner thyroid cartilage invasion) would make it T3. T2 N0 is stage II.

steps.label: Imaging
steps.prompt: Which scan is the workhorse for staging laryngeal cancer, and why?
choices: MRI, because it has the best soft-tissue detail
CT, because cartilage invasion defines the T-stage and CT shows bone and cartilage best
PET-CT, because it shows the primary tumor best
Ultrasound, because it shows cord movement
steps.explanation: Inner thyroid cartilage invasion is T3, and going through the outer cortex is T4a, so the laryngeal T-stage ladder is built on a CT finding. MRI is better for soft tissue and perineural spread, and PET-CT for nodes and distant disease.

steps.label: Treatment
steps.prompt: What is a standard definitive approach for him?
choices: Total laryngectomy and bilateral neck dissection
Definitive radiation to the larynx, without elective neck treatment
Chemoradiation to the larynx and both sides of the neck, levels I-V
Observation with a repeat scope in 3 months
steps.explanation: Early glottic cancer is treated with radiation to the larynx alone, or with larynx-preserving surgery (transoral or partial laryngectomy). A total laryngectomy would be far too much for a T2 cancer with a working larynx.

steps.label: Nodal levels
steps.prompt: Why is his neck not treated electively, when the neck would be treated for a T2 N0 supraglottic cancer?
choices: The glottis has almost no lymphatics, so the risk of hidden nodes is only about 5% for T2
Neck radiation is too toxic in smokers
The cricoid cartilage blocks lymphatic spread
Glottic cancer only spreads to level VI
steps.explanation: Nodal risk is about 2% for T1 and 5% for T2 glottic cancer. The supraglottis, in contrast, drains richly to both sides of the neck, so early supraglottic cancer gets bilateral levels II-IV.

steps.label: Counseling
steps.prompt: He asks what to expect during treatment and whether he can do anything to improve his chances. What do you tell him?
steps.answer: Expect a sore throat, a hoarse voice that often gets worse during treatment before it improves, redness of the skin on the front of the neck, and fatigue. Dry mouth is mild because the field is small. Stop smoking: smoking during RT worsens both tumor control and side effects.
steps.explanation: Also: no treatment breaks, because tumor repopulation means delays cost cure.

cases.title: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving
cases.oneLiner: A 49-year-old man who has never smoked noticed a painless lump on the left side of his neck while shaving. It has been there for 6 weeks and did not go away after a course of antibiotics.

steps.label: Exam
steps.prompt: On exam there is a 4 cm firm, mobile mass in the left upper neck (level II). Where should you look hardest for the primary tumor?
steps.explanation: A painless level II neck mass in a younger nonsmoker is the classic presentation of HPV-positive oropharynx cancer. The primary is often small or hidden in the tonsil or base of tongue. An adult neck mass that persists after antibiotics is cancer until proven otherwise.

steps.label: Imaging
steps.context: CT neck with contrast: a 4.2 cm cystic left level II node. No other enlarged nodes.
steps.caption: Axial contrast CT: a cystic left level II node (arrows) deep to the sternocleidomastoid, beside the internal jugular vein. Chengazi HU, Bhatt AA, Insights Imaging 2019 (PMC6377693), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: Fine-needle aspiration of the node shows squamous cell carcinoma. Which test on the tissue matters most next?
steps.explanation: p16 is the surrogate for HPV: the HPV E7 protein inactivates pRb, which drives p16 up. p16 status decides which staging system you use and frames prognosis. EBER testing is the move when the story points to the nasopharynx.

steps.label: Stage
steps.context: Scope and MRI: a 2.3 cm left tonsil mass that stays lateral; it does not reach the base of tongue or soft palate. Biopsy: nonkeratinizing squamous cell carcinoma, p16 positive. PET/CT: only the left tonsil and the single left level II node; no distant disease.
steps.caption: Axial MRI through the oropharynx: an asymmetric mass in one tonsillar region.
steps.prompt: Stage this cancer (AJCC 8th edition, p16-positive oropharynx).
steps.explanation: 2.3 cm is T2 (more than 2 and up to 4 cm). In p16-positive disease, any ipsilateral nodes all 6 cm or less are cN1, no matter how many. T2 N1 is stage I. If this same tumor were p16-negative, a single 4.2 cm node would be N2a, and the stage would jump to IVA.

steps.label: Treatment
steps.prompt: Which treatment is most appropriate off a clinical trial?
choices: Reduced-dose RT alone, because p16-positive cancer has a better prognosis
Definitive RT to about 70 Gy in 35 fractions with concurrent cisplatin
Induction chemotherapy alone, with no local treatment
steps.explanation: HPV changes the prognosis, not the treatment. With a node over 3 cm, NCCN options are concurrent chemoradiation or transoral surgery plus neck dissection; the goal is to pick one path and avoid triple therapy. De-escalated doses are only given on trials.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: He read online that cetuximab is gentler than cisplatin and asks to swap. Which trials answered this question for HPV-positive oropharynx cancer?
choices: The Tata Memorial neck dissection trial
steps.explanation: In RTOG 1016 and De-ESCALaTE, cetuximab with RT gave worse survival and more recurrences than cisplatin, without meaningfully less toxicity. Cisplatin stays the standard for patients who can take it.

steps.label: Nodal levels
steps.prompt: His tonsil primary is well lateralized. Which elective neck coverage fits?
choices: Both sides of the neck, levels II-IV
Left neck only: levels II-IV and VII (retropharyngeal), plus Ib and V because level II is involved
Left level II only, where the node is
Left levels II-IV, skipping level VII because it can't be felt on exam
steps.explanation: A well-lateralized tonsil cancer without base of tongue or soft palate involvement is the classic exception that allows one-sided neck treatment. Any pharyngeal primary adds level VII, and an involved level adds its neighbors (involved II: cover Ib and V) at an elective dose.

steps.label: Side effects
steps.caption: Oral mucositis during radiation for oropharyngeal cancer. Owosho AA et al., Dent J (Basel) 2023 (PMC10217705), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: What acute side effects of 7 weeks of chemoradiation to the oropharynx and neck should you counsel him about?
steps.answer: Mucositis and mouth and throat pain, painful swallowing with weight loss (sometimes a feeding tube), taste loss, dry mouth and thick saliva, a skin reaction on the neck, and fatigue; plus cisplatin effects such as nausea, kidney injury, hearing loss or ringing, and low blood counts.
steps.explanation: Mucositis peaks around weeks 4-6 and heals over the weeks after treatment. Late effects to preview: lasting dry mouth, taste change, swallowing problems, hypothyroidism, and osteoradionecrosis. Dental evaluation and fluoride trays come before RT starts.

cases.title: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear
cases.oneLiner: A 44-year-old man who grew up in Guangdong, China, has felt fullness in his right ear for 3 months. His doctor found fluid behind the right eardrum and treated it twice without improvement. He now has lumps on both sides of his neck.

steps.label: Localize
steps.prompt: An adult with fluid behind one eardrum and new neck nodes. Where is the primary most likely?
steps.explanation: One-sided serous otitis media in an adult means eustachian tube blockage until proven otherwise; scope the nasopharynx. Add his geography and neck nodes and this is the classic nasopharyngeal carcinoma story.

steps.label: Workup
steps.prompt: Which set of tests best completes his workup?
choices: Nasopharyngoscopy with biopsy, MRI of the skull base and neck, plasma EBV DNA, and PET/CT
p16 staining and a transoral robotic biopsy of the tonsil
steps.explanation: MRI is the modality of choice for the nasopharynx because skull base and perineural spread drive the T-stage. Plasma EBV DNA and EBER testing on the biopsy are the nasopharynx-specific additions. PET/CT checks nodes and distant disease, which matter in a cancer that presents with bulky nodes.

steps.label: Stage
steps.context: Endoscopy: a mass filling the right fossa of Rosenmüller. Biopsy: nonkeratinizing, undifferentiated carcinoma, EBER positive. MRI: tumor extends into the right parapharyngeal space; skull base intact; no intracranial spread. A right retropharyngeal node, bilateral level II nodes, and a right level V node, the largest 3.5 cm, all above the cricoid. PET/CT: no distant disease. Cranial nerve exam normal. Plasma EBV DNA: elevated.
steps.caption: FDG PET/CT: avid tumor filling the nasopharynx on axial, sagittal, and coronal fused views.
steps.prompt: Stage this cancer (AJCC 8th edition, nasopharynx).
steps.explanation: Parapharyngeal spread is T2 (bony skull base would be T3; intracranial or cranial nerve involvement T4). Bilateral cervical nodes 6 cm or less above the cricoid are N2. Retropharyngeal nodes, even on both sides, would only be N1. T2 N2 is stage III.

steps.label: Treatment
steps.prompt: What is the preferred treatment?
choices: Surgical resection of the nasopharynx, then RT
Induction gemcitabine and cisplatin, then concurrent cisplatin with RT
steps.explanation: The nasopharynx is not treated with surgery because the skull base is in the way; surgery is saved for salvage. RT alone is only for T1 N0. For node-positive disease, induction gemcitabine-cisplatin followed by concurrent cisplatin-RT is preferred.

steps.label: Nodal levels
steps.prompt: Which nodal coverage is right?
choices: Both sides, levels II-V, plus the retropharyngeal nodes (VII)
steps.explanation: Three rules stack here: any pharyngeal primary adds level VII, the nasopharynx is the one site that routinely adds level V, and a midline primary means both sides of the neck. The neck is always treated in nasopharynx cancer, even when it looks negative.

steps.label: Late effects
steps.prompt: Besides dry mouth, which late effects will you watch for, given that the target sits under the skull base, near the ears, and he is getting cisplatin?
steps.answer: Hearing loss (cisplatin plus dose to the cochlea, and lasting ear fluid), hypothyroidism from neck RT, temporal lobe injury, cranial nerve problems, trismus, and swallowing trouble.
steps.explanation: These are discussed before treatment and screened for afterward: audiograms, TSH checks, and a careful neuro and jaw exam at follow-up.

steps.label: Follow-up
steps.prompt: Which blood test helps track his response and watch for relapse?
steps.explanation: Plasma EBV DNA tracks the disease in nasopharyngeal carcinoma. A level that clears after treatment is reassuring, and a rising level suggests relapse.

cases.title: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal
cases.oneLiner: A 62-year-old woman who smoked for 40 years has had a painful sore on the side of her tongue for 2 months that she blamed on a sharp tooth. Filing the tooth down didn't help, and the pain now spreads to her left ear.

steps.label: Exam
steps.caption: An ulcerated lesion on the lateral border of the tongue. Dikkisherpa5, Wikimedia Commons, CC0.
steps.prompt: Biopsy shows invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Which imaging best measures the feature that drives T-stage at this site?
choices: CT, to measure depth of invasion
MRI, to measure depth of invasion
steps.explanation: The oral cavity is the only head and neck site where depth of invasion (DOI) is built into the T-stage. DOI is a soft-tissue measurement, so MRI is preferred; CT is better when the question is mandible cortex erosion.

steps.label: Imaging
steps.context: MRI: a 1.8 cm left lateral oral tongue tumor with a depth of invasion of about 7 mm, not crossing the midline. CT neck: no enlarged or necrotic nodes. CT chest: clear.
steps.caption: Axial contrast-enhanced T1 MRI of a left oral tongue cancer. J Korean Soc Radiol 2026 (PMC12883927), CC BY-NC 4.0.
steps.prompt: What is her clinical stage?
steps.explanation: The tumor is 2 cm or less, but DOI over 5 mm makes it T2 (DOI of 5 mm or less would be T1). A small but deep tumor can outstage a larger, superficial one. The DOI cutoffs to remember are 5 mm and 10 mm.

steps.label: Plan
steps.prompt: What is the primary treatment?
choices: Partial glossectomy with negative margins plus an elective neck dissection
Partial glossectomy alone, watching the neck
steps.explanation: Oral cavity cancer is surgery first. Her neck looks negative, but the neck is dissected anyway: the Tata Memorial trial showed better survival with an elective neck dissection than with waiting for a node to appear, especially when DOI is over about 3-4 mm.

steps.label: Pathology
steps.context: Left partial glossectomy and left neck dissection (levels I-III): 2.0 cm squamous cell carcinoma, DOI 8 mm, perineural invasion present, margins negative (closest 6 mm). 1 of 24 nodes positive (left level II, 1.4 cm), no extranodal extension.
steps.prompt: What is her pathologic stage, and what adjuvant treatment does she need?
steps.answer: pT2 N1 M0 (Stage III). Adjuvant radiation alone, about 60 Gy in 30 fractions, without chemo.
steps.explanation: Perineural invasion triggers adjuvant RT (framework step 2). Chemo is only added for a positive margin or extranodal extension (step 3), and she has neither. A single ipsilateral node of 3 cm or less without ENE is pN1.

steps.label: Nerve path
steps.prompt: Because of the perineural invasion, the radiation field may follow a nerve toward the skull base. Which one?
choices: The lingual nerve (V3), back toward the foramen ovale
The hypoglossal nerve, back toward the hypoglossal canal
The facial nerve, back toward the stylomastoid foramen
The recurrent laryngeal nerve, down into the chest
steps.explanation: PNI in the oral tongue tracks backward along V3 toward the foramen ovale and skull base, and it can carry tumor beyond what is visible. Her ear pain fits too: pain from the tongue can be referred to the ear along branches of V3.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: Change one detail: the positive node showed extranodal extension, so you add concurrent cisplatin. Which trials established that ENE or a positive margin is when chemo helps after surgery?
steps.explanation: Both trials asked whether adding cisplatin to postoperative RT helps high-risk patients. Their pooled analysis found a consistent benefit only for ECE/ENE and positive margins, which is framework step 3.

steps.label: Before RT
steps.prompt: Before her first fraction, which preventive visit is essential, and what late complication does it prevent?
steps.answer: A dental evaluation, with extraction of bad teeth before RT and lifelong fluoride trays, to prevent osteoradionecrosis of the mandible.
steps.explanation: Teeth pulled after RT heal poorly in irradiated bone. Speech and swallow evaluation, nutrition support, and smoking cessation round out the pre-treatment visits.

cases.title: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck
cases.oneLiner: A 64-year-old man with a 60 pack-year smoking history and heavy alcohol use has 3 months of sore throat, pain when swallowing, and a muffled voice. He has lost 15 pounds.

steps.label: Scope
steps.context: Laryngoscopy: a bulky right supraglottic mass involving the false cord and aryepiglottic fold and extending down to the glottis. The right vocal cord is fixed. His airway is adequate and he can still swallow liquids. Biopsy: squamous cell carcinoma, p16 negative.
steps.caption: Videoendoscopy of a right supraglottic tumor: swelling of the right false cord and aryepiglottic fold. Crosetti E et al., Front Oncol 2024 (PMC10847842), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: Which finding on this scope already makes the tumor at least T3?
steps.explanation: In the larynx, a fixed cord is T3 regardless of size, as is invasion of the paraglottic or pre-epiglottic space or the inner cortex of the thyroid cartilage. The neuro and scope exam is part of staging.

steps.label: Stage
steps.context: CT neck: tumor fills the right paraglottic space and the pre-epiglottic fat. The outer cortex of the thyroid cartilage is intact; no spread outside the larynx. Nodes: a 2.5 cm right level II node and a 2 cm left level III node, no ENE. PET/CT: no distant disease.
steps.prompt: Stage this cancer (AJCC 8th edition, supraglottis).
steps.explanation: Cord fixation and paraglottic and pre-epiglottic space invasion are T3; the outer thyroid cartilage cortex is intact, so it is not T4a. Nodes on both sides, none over 6 cm, are N2c. Any N2 is at least stage IVA.

steps.label: Key question
steps.prompt: Which question decides between total laryngectomy and organ preservation?
choices: Does the larynx still work, or is it destroyed?
Is the primary larger than 4 cm?
steps.explanation: Larynx cancer treatment is about organ preservation. A functional larynx goes to chemoradiation; a destroyed larynx (cartilage destruction, T4a, or a non-functional airway or swallow) goes to total laryngectomy.

steps.label: Treatment
steps.prompt: His larynx works and he wants to keep his voice. What is the best approach?
choices: Concurrent cisplatin-based chemoradiation to about 70 Gy
RT alone to the larynx, no neck
steps.explanation: For a T3 cancer with a working larynx, concurrent chemoradiation is the preferred organ-preservation approach. Induction chemo followed by RT or chemoRT, or total laryngectomy with neck dissection, are the alternatives.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: Which trial showed that concurrent chemoradiation gave the best larynx preservation (about 82% vs 64% with RT alone)?
steps.explanation: VA Larynx came first: induction chemo then RT matched surgery for survival, and 64% kept their larynx. RTOG 91-11 then compared induction, concurrent, and RT alone; concurrent chemoRT preserved the most larynges. Its main endpoint was laryngectomy-free survival, and overall survival was similar across arms.

steps.label: Nodal levels
steps.prompt: Which neck coverage fits?
choices: None, because the larynx has few lymphatics
Both sides, levels II-IV, with elective coverage of the levels next to the involved nodes
steps.explanation: This is the supraglottis, not the glottis: it drains richly to both sides of the neck. Involved nodes get full dose, and the levels next to them (for the right level II node, Ib and V) get an elective dose.

steps.label: What if
steps.caption: A different patient: axial contrast CT of an advanced laryngeal cancer destroying the cricoid and thyroid cartilages. Joshi VM et al., Indian J Radiol Imaging 2012 (PMC3624744), CC BY-NC-SA 3.0.
steps.prompt: Change one detail: CT shows tumor breaking through the outer cortex of the thyroid cartilage into the strap muscles. What now?
choices: Total laryngectomy and neck dissection, then adjuvant RT or chemoRT based on pathology
steps.explanation: Through the outer thyroid cartilage cortex is T4a, a destroyed larynx. Organ preservation works poorly here and often leaves a larynx that doesn't function, so surgery comes first; chemoRT is only for select patients who decline surgery.

cases.title: Case 7: Eight Months Later
cases.oneLiner: A 61-year-old man finished chemoradiation (70 Gy with weekly cisplatin) to his left tonsil and both sides of his neck 8 months ago. His 3-month PET/CT showed a complete response. He is in clinic today for routine follow-up.

steps.label: Surveillance
steps.prompt: Why was PET/CT, rather than CT alone, used for his first scan about 3 months after chemoradiation?
choices: Active tumor is FDG-avid while radiation scarring usually is not, so PET helps separate residual cancer from fibrosis
It shows the vocal cords in more detail
It avoids IV contrast, protecting the kidneys
steps.explanation: After treatment, CT and MRI often can't tell residual tumor from scar. Metabolically active tumor takes up FDG, while fibrosis and settled inflammation usually do not, which is why PET-CT is the post-treatment workhorse.

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.prompt: He has felt tired and cold all the time, has gained 8 pounds, and his skin is dry. What should you check first?
steps.explanation: Hypothyroidism is common after neck radiation because the thyroid sits in the low neck field. It usually shows up months to years after treatment, so TSH is checked regularly in follow-up and replaced with levothyroxine when low.

steps.label: Dry mouth
steps.prompt: His mouth is still very dry, and he carries a water bottle everywhere. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Dry mouth always resolves fully by 3 months after RT
Dry mouth is often a lasting late effect of dose to the parotid glands, and it raises his risk of cavities
Dry mouth at 8 months means the cancer is back
Dry mouth is caused only by the cisplatin
steps.explanation: Saliva loss from parotid dose can be permanent; IMRT reduces it by sparing the parotids. Less saliva means more cavities, which is one reason fluoride trays are lifelong.

steps.label: Dental
steps.prompt: He has a painful lower left molar, and a community dentist wants to pull it this week. What is the main risk, and what should happen instead?
steps.answer: Osteoradionecrosis of the mandible: irradiated bone heals poorly, so an extraction can leave exposed, dead bone. He should see a dentist experienced with irradiated patients, save the tooth if possible, and if it must come out, have it removed as gently as possible with ORN precautions.
steps.explanation: This is why bad teeth are extracted before RT, and why the dental team stays involved for life.

steps.label: Complication
steps.caption: Exposed necrotic bone where a lower left molar was lost, in a patient treated with radiation for left tonsil cancer. Owosho AA et al., Dent J (Basel) 2023 (PMC10217705), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: The tooth was pulled at an outside office anyway. Two months later he has jaw pain and this exam. What is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.explanation: Exposed, non-healing bone in an irradiated field after a dental extraction is osteoradionecrosis. Still biopsy anything that looks like a mass or a suspicious ulcer, because recurrence can mimic it.

steps.label: Red flag
steps.prompt: At a later visit, which new finding should most raise concern for recurrence rather than a treatment effect?
choices: A new, growing, firm neck mass with new ear pain on the treated side
Stable firmness of the neck skin
steps.explanation: Most recurrences happen within the first 2 years. New pain, ear pain, a growing mass, or bleeding prompts a scope and imaging, and PET-CT helps separate tumor from fibrosis or neuritis.

cases.title: Case 8: Can't Open Wide
cases.oneLiner: A 59-year-old man who smokes and chews tobacco has 3 months of right jaw pain. Over the last month he can barely open his mouth, and the right side of his lower lip and chin have gone numb.

steps.label: Exam
steps.caption: How trismus is measured: maximal mouth opening of about 6 mm with a ruler between the incisors (shown in a patient after head and neck radiation). Owosho AA et al., Dent J (Basel) 2023 (PMC10217705), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: He can only open his mouth about this far. What does new trismus suggest about a tumor in this region?
choices: Involvement of the pterygoid muscles and masticator space
steps.explanation: The pterygoid muscles open and close the jaw. New trouble opening the mouth means the tumor has reached them, and masticator space invasion is T4b in the oral cavity.

steps.label: Numb chin
steps.prompt: Which nerve explains numbness of his lower lip and chin?
choices: The inferior alveolar and mental nerves (V3)
The marginal mandibular branch of CN VII
steps.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve runs through the mandible and exits as the mental nerve to supply the lower lip and chin. A numb chin means mandible invasion or perineural spread along V3. The marginal mandibular branch is motor (lip asymmetry), not sensory.

steps.label: Stage
steps.context: Exam: an ulcerated mass behind the last right lower molar (retromolar trigone). CT: erosion through the cortex of the right mandible. MRI: tumor extends into the right medial and lateral pterygoid muscles and the masticator space; the right V3 nerve is thickened and enhancing, and the foramen ovale is widened. Nodes: a 2.5 cm right level Ib node and a 2 cm right level II node, no ENE. PET/CT: no distant disease.
steps.caption: Axial contrast CT: a retromolar trigone cancer eroding the right mandible. Jones W et al., Oral Oncol Rep 2025 (PMC12199806), CC BY-NC 4.0.
steps.prompt: Stage this cancer (AJCC 8th edition, oral cavity).
steps.explanation: Erosion through the mandibular cortex alone would be T4a, which is still resectable. Masticator space, pterygoid involvement, or skull base spread makes it T4b. Multiple ipsilateral nodes, none over 6 cm, are N2b. Any T4b is stage IVB.

steps.label: Imaging
steps.prompt: Which of these is NOT an MRI sign of perineural spread?
choices: Loss of the fat around the nerve
steps.explanation: Nerve thickening, foraminal widening, loss of perineural fat, and abnormal nerve enhancement are the signs to know. A cystic level II node is a classic HPV-positive oropharynx finding, not a perineural sign.

steps.label: Treatment
steps.prompt: Tumor board agrees the tumor is unresectable. What is the treatment?
choices: Definitive concurrent chemoradiation (about 70 Gy with cisplatin), induction chemo followed by chemoRT, or a clinical trial
Palliative RT alone, 20 Gy in 5 fractions
steps.explanation: T4b disease, unresectable nodes, or an unfit patient means definitive chemoradiation to about 70 Gy, induction chemo followed by RT or chemoRT, or a clinical trial. RT alone is for patients who can't take chemo.

steps.label: Target
steps.prompt: Besides the gross tumor and involved nodes, what else must be in the radiation target?
steps.answer: The path of V3 back through the foramen ovale to the skull base (perineural spread), the whole masticator space, and the elective neck: at least the right levels I-IV plus the levels next to the involved Ib and II nodes, with the left neck based on how close the disease comes to midline.
steps.explanation: Perineural spread can carry tumor beyond what is visible, so the field follows the nerve. Lateralized oral cavity tumors can sometimes be treated on one side, but bulky, deep disease like this often gets both sides.

steps.label: Late risk
steps.prompt: Given where this tumor sits, which late complication is he at highest risk for?
choices: Osteoradionecrosis of the mandible and worsening trismus
steps.explanation: High dose to a mandible that the tumor has already eroded, plus poor dentition and tobacco, means a high ORN risk. Prevention: dental extractions before RT, lifelong fluoride, quitting tobacco, and daily jaw-stretching exercises to fight trismus.
